name: Haryanka dynasty
rise: Bimbisara (r. c. 544–492 BCE) built Magadha's power by marriage alliances with Kosala, the Licchavis and Madra, and by annexing Anga, which gave him the port of Champa and Ganga trade. He organised officials to collect land revenue directly. His son Ajatashatru fought a long war against the Vajji confederacy, reportedly using new weapons such as a catapult and a scythed chariot, and fortified the village of Pataligrama, later Pataliputra.
fall: Haryanka kings are remembered in Buddhist texts as patricides: Ajatashatru is said to have killed Bimbisara, and his successors killed their fathers in turn. Disgusted, the people and ministers deposed the last Haryanka king, Nagadasaka, and raised the minister Shishunaga to the throne around 413 BCE.

name: Nanda Empire
rise: Mahapadma Nanda, said by Puranas to be the son of a Shudra woman, overthrew the Shishunagas and defeated many older kshatriya dynasties, earning the title 'destroyer of all kshatriyas'. The Nandas built the first huge standing army in India — Greek sources speak of 200,000 infantry, 20,000 cavalry, 2,000 chariots and 3,000–6,000 elephants — which deterred Alexander's tired troops from crossing the Beas in 326 BCE.
fall: Heavy taxation and the low-born status ascribed to them made the Nandas unpopular. Tradition says the Brahmin Chanakya, insulted at Dhana Nanda's court, trained the young Chandragupta Maurya, who raised an army in the northwest and overthrew Dhana Nanda around 322 BCE.

name: Maurya dynasty
rise: Chandragupta Maurya, advised by the Brahmin strategist Chanakya, overthrew the unpopular Nanda dynasty of Magadha around 322 BCE, after Alexander's withdrawal from Punjab left a power vacuum in the northwest. In about 303 BCE he defeated or made peace with Seleucus I, gaining Afghanistan and Baluchistan in exchange for 500 war elephants. His son Bindusara expanded into the Deccan, and Ashoka conquered Kalinga (261 BCE), bringing almost the whole subcontinent except the far south under one rule.
fall: After Ashoka's death in 232 BCE the empire split between successors, provinces broke away, and revenue fell. Some historians blame the costs of a vast bureaucracy and army; others cite Ashoka's pacifism weakening the military, though this is disputed. In 185 BCE the general Pushyamitra Shunga assassinated the last Mauryan king, Brihadratha, during an army review and founded the Shunga dynasty, while Indo-Greeks invaded from the northwest.

name: Shunga dynasty
rise: In about 185 BCE the commander-in-chief Pushyamitra Shunga assassinated the last Maurya emperor, Brihadratha, during a military parade and took the throne. He performed Vedic horse sacrifices (ashvamedha) to proclaim sovereignty and fought off Indo-Greek raids; his grandson Vasumitra defeated Greeks on the Sindhu river.
fall: The Shunga realm shrank to Magadha and central India (Vidisha). Its last king Devabhuti was killed in a palace plot by his minister Vasudeva Kanva around 73 BCE, who founded the short-lived Kanva dynasty. Shunga-era art survives on the Bharhut stupa and the Sanchi gateways' early phases.

name: Indo-Greek kingdoms
rise: Greek kingdoms of Bactria, left over from Alexander's conquest and the Seleucid empire, crossed the Hindu Kush around 200 BCE under Demetrius I as Mauryan power faded. Menander I (Milinda, r. c. 165–130 BCE) ruled from Sagala (Sialkot) and is remembered in the Buddhist Milindapanha dialogue with the monk Nagasena.
fall: The Indo-Greeks fragmented into some 30 rival kings and were squeezed by Scythians (Sakas), Parthians and finally the Kushans; the last ruler, Strato II, disappears around 10 CE. They left bilingual Greek–Kharosthi coins with realistic portraits and contributed to Gandhara art.

name: Satavahana dynasty
rise: After the Mauryas declined, Simuka founded the dynasty around the 1st century BCE in the western Deccan.
fall: Wars with the Western Kshatrapas and internal division split the realm into smaller kingdoms by the early 3rd century.

name: Western Kshatrapas
rise: Saka (Scythian) governors who had served the Kushans established themselves in Gujarat, Malwa and Saurashtra in the 1st century CE. Rudradaman I (r. c. 130–150) defeated the Satavahanas twice and left the Junagadh rock inscription (150 CE) — the earliest long inscription in Sanskrit — recording repairs to the Mauryan Sudarshana lake.
fall: Gupta emperor Chandragupta II conquered them around 395–415 CE, gaining the rich ports of western India; legend links this victory to the hero Vikramaditya. Their dated coins are a key source for Indian chronology.

name: Gupta dynasty
rise: The Guptas began as a minor family in Magadha. Chandragupta I (r. ~320–335) married Kumaradevi, a princess of the powerful Licchavi clan, which raised his status. His son Samudragupta (r. ~335–375), celebrated in the Allahabad pillar inscription, conquered or subdued kings across northern India and received tribute from the south. Chandragupta II (r. ~375–415) defeated the Western Kshatrapas, gaining Gujarat's sea trade.
fall: From around 460 CE the Alchon Huns (Hunas) invaded from Central Asia. Skandagupta repelled them at first, but later attacks under Toramana and Mihirakula devastated the northwest and drained the treasury. At the same time feudatories such as the Maukharis and Maitrakas became independent, trade with the Roman world declined, and the dynasty faded by around 550.

name: Vakataka dynasty
rise: Founded by Vindhyashakti around 250 CE in the Deccan after the Satavahanas collapsed, the Vakatakas performed Vedic sacrifices and ruled central India. Chandragupta II married his daughter Prabhavatigupta to the Vakataka king; as regent she ruled for years, binding the two dynasties.
fall: The kingdom split into two branches, which declined in the late 5th century under pressure from neighbours such as the Vishnukundins and Kalachuris. Their great legacy is the later Ajanta caves, sponsored under King Harishena (r. c. 460–478).

name: Pushyabhuti (Vardhana) dynasty
rise: The Pushyabhutis ruled Thanesar (Haryana) and rose by fighting the Hunas. Harshavardhana (r. 606–647) took over Kannauj after his sister's husband was killed, uniting most of north India. Xuanzang described his huge assemblies at Prayag, where Harsha gave away all his wealth every five years.
fall: Harsha was defeated by Pulakeshin II on the Narmada (c. 618) and left no heir; after his death in 647 a minister usurped the throne and the empire disintegrated. Kannauj became the prize fought over by Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas.

name: Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty
rise: Nagabhata I (c. 730–760) won fame by repelling Arab armies from Sindh, protecting western India. His successors took Kannauj (c. 816) and under Mihira Bhoja (r. 836–885) ruled from Gujarat to Bengal; the Arab traveller Sulaiman called them hostile to Islam but praised their security.
fall: A century of tripartite struggle with Palas and Rashtrakutas exhausted them; Rashtrakuta Indra III sacked Kannauj in 916. Mahmud of Ghazni's raid in 1018 broke them, and smaller Rajput clans (Chandela, Paramara, Chauhan) succeeded.

name: Pala dynasty
rise: Gopala's election around 750; Dharmapala and Devapala expanded the realm across north India.
fall: Weakened by Pratihara and Rashtrakuta wars, they were overthrown by the Senas in the 12th century.

name: Rashtrakuta dynasty
rise: Dantidurga, a Chalukya feudatory, overthrew Kirtivarman II around 753 and founded the Rashtrakuta dynasty in the Deccan. His successor Krishna I commissioned the monolithic Kailasa temple at Ellora. Dhruva and Govinda III raided as far as Kannauj, and Amoghavarsha I (r. 814–878), who reigned 64 years, founded the capital Manyakheta and wrote the Kannada poetics work Kavirajamarga.
fall: Their wars with Pratiharas, Palas, Cholas and Eastern Chalukyas were endless. Krishna III won a great victory over the Cholas at Takkolam (949), but soon after Paramara king Siyaka sacked Manyakheta (972). A feudatory, Tailapa II, overthrew the last Rashtrakuta king in 973, founding the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani.

name: Chola dynasty (Imperial)
rise: The early Cholas appear in Sangam literature, but the Imperial Cholas began when Vijayalaya captured Thanjavur from the Muttaraiyars around 848. Rajaraja I (985–1014) conquered the Cheras, Pandyas, northern Sri Lanka and the Maldives; his son Rajendra I (1014–1044) marched to the Ganga, founding Gangaikonda Cholapuram ('city of the Chola who conquered the Ganga'), and sent a naval expedition against the Srivijaya empire in 1025.
fall: Long wars with the Western Chalukyas drained resources. In the 12th–13th centuries, provincial chiefs grew powerful, the Pandyas revived in the south and the Hoysalas in the west. The last Chola king, Rajendra III, was defeated by the Pandya Jatavarman Sundara Pandyan around 1279.

name: Western Chalukyas (Kalyani)
rise: Tailapa II, a Rashtrakuta feudatory claiming Chalukya descent, overthrew his overlords in 973 and ruled from Kalyani. His dynasty fought long wars with the Cholas over the Raichur doab. Vikramaditya VI (r. 1076–1126) started his own era and patronised the poet Bilhana and jurist Vijnaneshwara, author of the Mitakshara law commentary.
fall: Feudatories grew powerful — the Kalachuris seized Kalyani in 1157, and Hoysalas, Yadavas and Kakatiyas divided the realm by 1189. Their ornate temples in Lakkundi and Itagi developed the Kalyani Chalukya style.

name: Hoysala Empire
rise: Hill chiefs from the Malnad region of Karnataka, the Hoysalas served as Chalukya feudatories and became independent under Vishnuvardhana (r. 1108–1152), who reportedly converted from Jainism to Vaishnavism under Ramanuja.
fall: They were caught between Pandyas and Yadavas, and the Delhi Sultanate's general Malik Kafur sacked their capital Dwarasamudra in 1311. Veera Ballala III died fighting the Madurai Sultanate in 1343; his officers Harihara and Bukka helped found Vijayanagara. Their star-shaped temples at Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura are UNESCO-listed.

name: Kakatiya dynasty
rise: Kakatiyas were Chalukya feudatories in Telangana who became independent under Prola II and Rudra I (c. 1163). Ganapati (r. 1199–1262) and his daughter Rudramadevi, one of India's few reigning queens, built Warangal fort and the Thousand Pillar and Ramappa temples, and an irrigation system of tanks.
fall: The Delhi Sultanate attacked repeatedly; Muhammad bin Tughlaq (then Ulugh Khan) captured Warangal in 1323 and took Prataparudra prisoner. The Kakatiya tanks and Ramappa temple (UNESCO 2021) remain.

name: Eastern Ganga dynasty
rise: Anantavarman Chodaganga (r. 1078–1147) ruled from the Godavari to the Ganga and began the Jagannath temple at Puri. Narasimhadeva I (r. 1238–1264) defeated Bengal's Muslim rulers and built the Sun Temple at Konark, conceived as a giant stone chariot with 24 wheels.
fall: Weakened by Delhi and Bengal sultanates and internal revolts, the last Ganga king was overthrown in 1434 by his minister Kapilendra Deva, founder of the Gajapati dynasty.

name: Mamluk (Slave) dynasty
rise: Qutb ud-Din Aibak, a Turkic slave who rose as Muhammad of Ghor's general, ruled from Delhi from 1206. Iltutmish (r. 1211–1236) consolidated the Sultanate, received caliphal recognition and introduced silver tanka and copper jital coins; his daughter Razia (r. 1236–40) was the only woman to rule Delhi. Balban (r. 1266–87) held off the Mongols with harsh rule.
fall: After Balban's death his weak grandson Kaiqubad was killed, and the Khalji nobles took power in 1290.

name: Khalji dynasty
rise: Jalaluddin Khalji seized power in 1290, ending the Turkish nobles' monopoly. His nephew Alauddin murdered him in 1296 and, with the loot of Devagiri, made himself sultan. Alauddin defeated several Mongol invasions, introduced market price controls, and sent Malik Kafur on raids to Warangal, Dwarasamudra and Madurai.
fall: After Alauddin's death in 1316, Malik Kafur's brief regency and the murders of rival princes led to the rise of Khusrau Khan, killed by Ghazi Malik (Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq) in 1320.

name: Tughlaq dynasty
rise: Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq founded the dynasty in 1320 and built Tughlaqabad. Muhammad bin Tughlaq (r. 1325–51) was brilliant but erratic: token currency, a move of capital to Daulatabad and a planned conquest of Khurasan all failed. Firuz Shah (r. 1351–88) built canals, towns and hospitals.
fall: Revolts produced the Bahmani Sultanate and Vijayanagara (1336–47). Timur sacked Delhi in 1398, killing tens of thousands; the dynasty limped on until 1414.

name: Lodi dynasty
rise: Bahlul Lodi, an Afghan governor, took the throne in 1451. Sikandar Lodi (r. 1489–1517) founded Agra and made it his capital.
fall: Ibrahim Lodi alienated Afghan nobles, who invited Babur from Kabul. Babur's field guns and tactics defeated him at the First Battle of Panipat (1526).

name: Bahmani Sultanate
rise: Founded in 1347 by Alauddin Bahman Shah, who rebelled against Muhammad bin Tughlaq, with capitals at Gulbarga and Bidar. Minister Mahmud Gawan reformed administration and built a madrasa in Bidar.
fall: Factional conflict between Deccani and foreign nobles, and Gawan's execution in 1481, led to five successor sultanates: Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Berar and Bidar.

name: Sangama, Saluva and Tuluva dynasties (Vijayanagara)
rise: Brothers Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama family founded the empire in 1336 to resist the Delhi Sultanate's raids into the south.
fall: An alliance of the Deccan sultanates defeated Vijayanagara at Talikota in 1565; Hampi was sacked for months. The dynasty continued weakly until 1646.

name: Mughal dynasty
rise: Babur, a Timurid prince from Fergana descended from both Timur and Genghis Khan, invaded India and defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat (1526) and Rana Sanga at Khanwa (1527). His son Humayun lost the empire to Sher Shah Suri (1540) and regained it in 1555. Akbar (r. 1556–1605) won the Second Battle of Panipat and built a stable empire through conquest, alliances and reforms.
fall: Aurangzeb (r. 1658–1707) expanded the empire to its largest extent but spent 25 years at war in the Deccan against the Marathas, emptying the treasury, while reimposing the jizya alienated many subjects. After his death, wars of succession, rebellious governors (Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad), Maratha expansion, Sikh and Jat revolts, Nadir Shah's devastating sack of Delhi (1739) and Afghan invasions shattered central power. The East India Company reduced the emperors to pensioners, and the last emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, was exiled after 1857.

name: Suri dynasty
rise: Sher Shah Suri, an Afghan commander, defeated the Mughal Humayun at Chausa (1539) and Kannauj (1540) and ruled north India. He introduced the silver rupiya, land measurement, and rebuilt the Grand Trunk Road with caravanserais.
fall: Sher Shah died in a gunpowder explosion in 1545. Succession quarrels let Humayun return; Akbar's general defeated Hemu at the Second Battle of Panipat (1556).

name: Rajput kingdoms of Mewar (Sisodia)
notable: Rana Kumbha, Rana Sanga, Maharana Pratap
rise: Hammir Singh recaptured Chittor around 1326 after Alauddin Khalji's siege of 1303. Rana Kumbha (r. 1433–68) built the Vijay Stambh and Kumbhalgarh fort; Rana Sanga united Rajputs against Babur.
fall: Mewar never fully submitted: Maharana Pratap fought Akbar at Haldighati (1576). It accepted Mughal suzerainty in 1615 and British protection in 1818, and merged into India in 1948.

name: Ahom dynasty
rise: The Tai prince Sukaphaa crossed the Patkai hills in 1228 and united local peoples.
fall: Civil war, Burmese invasions (1817–1826) and British annexation after the Treaty of Yandabo (1826).

name: Maratha Empire (Bhonsle and Peshwas)
rise: Shivaji (1630–1680) built a state in the Western Ghats by seizing Bijapur forts, defeated Afzal Khan (1659), escaped from Aurangzeb's custody at Agra (1666) and was crowned Chhatrapati in 1674. After Aurangzeb's death the Marathas expanded across India under Peshwa Bajirao I.
fall: Defeat by Ahmad Shah Durrani at the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) cost a generation of leaders. Internal rivalries let the British win three Anglo-Maratha Wars; the confederacy ended in 1818.

name: Sikh Empire (Sukerchakia)
rise: Ranjit Singh unified the Sikh misls and captured Lahore in 1799, then Multan, Kashmir and Peshawar.
fall: After his death in 1839, court intrigue and assassinations weakened the state; the British won the Anglo-Sikh Wars (1845–46, 1848–49) and annexed Punjab.

name: Mysore (Wodeyar and Hyder Ali)
rise: Hyder Ali seized power from the Wodeyars and expanded Mysore across the south.
fall: Four Anglo-Mysore Wars; Tipu died defending Srirangapatna in 1799, and the British restored the Wodeyars as subordinate rulers.

name: Nizams of Hyderabad (Asaf Jahi)
rise: Asaf Jah I, the Mughal viceroy of the Deccan, became independent in 1724. Later Nizams allied with the British as a 'subsidiary' state.
fall: The last Nizam, Osman Ali Khan, one of the world's richest men, refused to join India; Operation Polo (1948) integrated Hyderabad.

name: Achaemenid dynasty
rise: Cyrus the Great overthrew the Medes (550 BCE), conquered Lydia and Babylon (539 BCE), and his successors took Egypt and northwest India.
fall: Costly wars with Greece, palace intrigue and revolts weakened it; Alexander defeated Darius III at Issus and Gaugamela (331 BCE).

name: Seleucid dynasty
rise: Seleucus I, Alexander's general, took Babylon in 312 BCE and built an empire from Anatolia to Bactria; he traded India's eastern provinces to Chandragupta for 500 elephants. Antioch became a great city.
fall: Parthians and Bactrians broke away; Rome defeated Antiochus III at Magnesia (190 BCE). Pompey annexed Syria in 63 BCE.

name: Parthian Empire
rise: Arsaces I led the Parni nomads to seize Parthia around 247 BCE; Mithridates I conquered Mesopotamia. Parthian horse archers destroyed a Roman army at Carrhae (53 BCE).
fall: Repeated Roman invasions and civil wars weakened them; their vassal Ardashir I of Persis killed the last king in 224 CE.

name: Sasanian Empire
rise: Ardashir I founded the empire in 224, promoting Zoroastrianism as state religion. Shapur I captured the Roman emperor Valerian (260). Khosrow I (r. 531–579) reformed taxes and welcomed scholars.
fall: An exhausting war with Byzantium (602–628) and civil war left them weak against the Arab armies, which won at Qadisiyya (636) and Nahavand (642).

name: Rashidun Caliphate
rise: After Muhammad's death in 632, Abu Bakr was chosen caliph and reunited Arabia. Umar's armies conquered Syria, Egypt, Iraq and Persia.
fall: Uthman was killed in 656; the first civil war between Ali and Muawiya followed, and Ali was murdered in 661.

name: Umayyad Caliphate
rise: Muawiya founded the Umayyad dynasty in Damascus. Its armies reached Spain (711) and Sindh (712). Abd al-Malik built the Dome of the Rock and made Arabic the administrative language.
fall: Non-Arab Muslims resented their status; the Abbasid revolution defeated them on the Zab in 750. An Umayyad prince founded the Emirate of Córdoba.

name: Abbasid Caliphate
rise: Founded on the Abbasid revolution in 750; al-Mansur founded Baghdad in 762. Under Harun al-Rashid and al-Mamun the House of Wisdom translated Greek and Indian works.
fall: Provincial dynasties split away, Turkish soldiers took control, and the Mongols under Hulagu sacked Baghdad in 1258.

name: Fatimid Caliphate
rise: Ismaili Shia leader al-Mahdi founded the caliphate in Tunisia (909); they conquered Egypt in 969 and founded Cairo and al-Azhar.
fall: Crusades, famine and military feuds; Saladin abolished it in 1171.

name: Seljuk Empire
rise: Tughril Beg led Oghuz Turks to take Baghdad in 1055. Alp Arslan defeated Byzantium at Manzikert (1071), opening Anatolia to Turks; vizier Nizam al-Mulk founded madrasas.
fall: It fragmented after Malik Shah's death (1092); the Khwarazmians defeated the last Great Seljuk in 1194.

name: Ayyubid dynasty
rise: Saladin, a Kurdish general, ended the Fatimids, united Egypt and Syria, and recaptured Jerusalem in 1187.
fall: Family rivalries; Mamluk soldiers killed the last sultan in 1250.

name: Mamluk Sultanate (Egypt)
rise: Turkic and Circassian slave soldiers (mamluks) killed the last Ayyubid sultan in 1250. They defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut (1260) under Baybars and expelled the last crusaders (Acre, 1291); Cairo became the Islamic world's greatest city.
fall: Plague, Portuguese disruption of the spice trade and outdated tactics weakened them; Selim I's Ottoman artillery won at Marj Dabiq (1516) and Ridaniya (1517).

name: Ilkhanate
rise: Hulagu Khan, Genghis Khan's grandson, destroyed the Assassins' fortresses and sacked Baghdad (1258), killing the last Abbasid caliph, and founded the Ilkhanate in Persia and Iraq. Ghazan Khan converted to Islam (1295), and his vizier Rashid al-Din wrote the Jami al-Tawarikh, the first world history.
fall: The Mamluks stopped Ilkhanid expansion at Ain Jalut (1260). Abu Said died in 1335 without an heir, and the realm split into regional dynasties such as the Jalayirids and Muzaffarids, later swept up by Timur.

name: Timurid Empire
rise: Timur conquered from Delhi to Anatolia and made Samarkand dazzling. His grandson Ulugh Beg built an observatory.
fall: Divided among heirs; Uzbeks took Samarkand in 1500–07. Babur founded the Mughal Empire.

name: Ottoman dynasty
rise: Osman I's frontier principality in Anatolia expanded into the Balkans; Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453; Selim I took Egypt and Arabia; Suleiman reached Vienna (1529).
fall: Military defeats from 1683, nationalism in the Balkans, economic dependence on Europe and defeat in World War I led to its dissolution and the Turkish Republic (1923).

name: Safavid dynasty
rise: Ismail I, head of a Sufi order, took Tabriz (1501) and imposed Shia Islam. Shah Abbas I (r. 1588–1629) moved the capital to Isfahan.
fall: Weak shahs and the Afghan siege of Isfahan (1722); Nader Shah ended the dynasty in 1736.

name: Qajar dynasty
rise: Agha Mohammad Khan, a Turkmen chief, reunited Iran by 1794 and made Tehran his capital.
fall: Losses to Russia, concessions to foreigners, the 1906 Constitutional Revolution, and Reza Khan's coup (1921) led to their deposition in 1925.

name: Kushan dynasty
rise: The Yuezhi nomads, pushed from China's frontier, conquered Bactria; Kujula Kadphises united them in the 1st century CE.
fall: Defeats by the Sasanians in the 3rd century and the rise of the Guptas in India reduced them to minor rulers.

name: Hephthalites (White Huns)
rise: Central Asian nomads who defeated the Sasanians in 484 and, under Toramana and Mihirakula, raided Gupta India.
fall: Yashodharman defeated Mihirakula around 528; the Sasanians and Turks crushed them around 560.

name: Göktürk Khaganate
rise: Bumin Qaghan revolted against the Rouran (552). The Orkhon inscriptions are the earliest written Turkic.
fall: Divided into east and west, then destroyed by the Uyghurs in 744.

name: Xia dynasty (traditional)
rise: The Shang overthrew the semi-legendary Xia around 1600 BCE according to tradition.
fall: The last Shang king, remembered as a tyrant, was defeated by the Zhou around 1046 BCE.

name: Shang dynasty
rise: The Shang overthrew the semi-legendary Xia around 1600 BCE according to tradition.
fall: The last Shang king, remembered as a tyrant, was defeated by the Zhou around 1046 BCE.

name: Zhou dynasty
rise: King Wu of Zhou defeated the last Shang king at Muye around 1046 BCE.
fall: Nomad attacks and rebellion forced the move east in 771 BCE; afterwards the Zhou kings were figureheads until Qin extinguished them in 256 BCE.

name: Qin dynasty
rise: Qin, a western state, became powerful after Shang Yang's Legalist reforms (4th century BCE). King Ying Zheng conquered the other six Warring States by 221 BCE and named himself First Emperor.
fall: Massive forced labour, harsh laws and book burning provoked hatred. After the First Emperor died in 210 BCE, the Chen Sheng–Wu Guang uprising and other rebellions brought down the dynasty by 206 BCE.

name: Han dynasty
rise: Liu Bang, a peasant-born official, rebelled after the Qin collapse and defeated the aristocrat Xiang Yu in 202 BCE, founding the Han. He softened Qin's harsh laws while keeping its centralised structure.
fall: Land concentration, court intrigue between eunuchs and consort families, and natural disasters led to the Yellow Turban rebellion (184 CE). Warlords who suppressed it carved up China; in 220 the last Han emperor abdicated, beginning the Three Kingdoms.

name: Sui dynasty
rise: Yang Jian (Emperor Wen) reunified China in 589 and restored examinations.
fall: Emperor Yang's Grand Canal and failed Korean wars caused revolts; Tang took over in 618.

name: Tang dynasty
rise: After the short Sui dynasty reunified China (581) but exhausted it with huge canal projects and failed wars in Korea, rebellions broke out. Li Yuan, a Sui general, and his son Li Shimin captured Chang'an and founded the Tang in 618. Li Shimin, as Emperor Taizong (r. 626–649), defeated the Eastern Turks, extended control along the Silk Road into Central Asia, and governed so effectively his reign became a byword for good rule.
fall: In 751 the Tang lost to the Abbasids at the Battle of Talas, ending expansion westward. In 755 the general An Lushan rebelled; the eight-year An Lushan rebellion devastated the north and may have cost millions of lives. Afterwards provincial military governors (jiedushi) became semi-independent, eunuchs dominated the court, and the equal-field system collapsed. The Huang Chao rebellion (874–884) sacked Chang'an, and in 907 the warlord Zhu Wen deposed the last Tang emperor, opening the Five Dynasties period.

name: Song dynasty
rise: General Zhao Kuangyin was proclaimed emperor by his troops in 960 and reunified most of China, ending the Five Dynasties chaos.
fall: The Song lost the north to the Jurchen Jin in 1127 and moved its capital to Hangzhou. The Mongols conquered the Jin, then besieged Song cities for decades; the last Song emperor died at the naval Battle of Yamen in 1279.

name: Yuan dynasty
rise: Genghis Khan's Mongols attacked the Jin from 1211. His grandson Kublai declared the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and destroyed the Southern Song in 1279, the first time a non-Chinese people ruled all of China.
fall: Failed invasions of Japan (1274, 1281) and Java drained the treasury, and paper-money inflation and Yellow River floods followed. Plague and ethnic discrimination fuelled the Red Turban revolts. Zhu Yuanzhang took Dadu in 1368 and the Mongols withdrew to the steppe.

name: Ming dynasty
rise: Zhu Yuanzhang, a peasant orphan and former monk, led the Red Turban rebellion against the Mongol Yuan and founded the Ming in 1368.
fall: Bureaucratic paralysis, eunuch corruption, costly wars in Korea against Japan, silver shortages, Little Ice Age famines and epidemics led to peasant revolts. Rebel Li Zicheng took Beijing in 1644; the last emperor hanged himself, and the Manchus swept in as the Qing.

name: Qing dynasty
rise: The Manchus, unified by Nurhaci, took Beijing in 1644 after the Ming collapse.
fall: Population pressure, corruption, the Opium Wars (1839–42, 1856–60), the Taiping Rebellion (1850–64) and other revolts, unequal treaties, defeat by Japan (1895), and the Boxer Rebellion (1900) undermined the dynasty. The 1911 Xinhai Revolution ended over 2,000 years of imperial rule.

name: Yamato and imperial Japan
rise: The Yamato kingdom unified Japan in the 3rd–6th centuries; the emperor line is the world's oldest hereditary monarchy.
fall: Not fallen; the 1947 constitution made the emperor a symbol of the state.

name: Kamakura shogunate
rise: Minamoto no Yoritomo won the Genpei War and in 1192 was named shogun, creating rule by warriors from Kamakura; the Hōjō family later ruled as regents.
fall: Repelling the Mongol invasions (1274, 1281) left warriors unrewarded; Emperor Go-Daigo's revolt with Ashikaga Takauji ended it in 1333.

name: Tokugawa shogunate
rise: Tokugawa Ieyasu won the Battle of Sekigahara (1600) and became shogun in 1603, ending a century of civil war.
fall: Commodore Perry's US ships (1853) forced Japan open. Unequal treaties and domestic unrest followed, and samurai from Satsuma and Chōshū overthrew the shogunate in the Meiji Restoration (1868).

name: Goryeo
rise: Wang Geon reunified Korea in 918; Goryeo printed the Tripitaka Koreana and the first metal movable type (Jikji, 1377).
fall: Mongol domination and Yi Seong-gye's coup (1392).

name: Joseon dynasty
rise: General Yi Seong-gye overthrew the Goryeo dynasty in 1392 and moved the capital to Hanyang (Seoul).
fall: Japanese (1592–98) and Manchu (1627, 1636) invasions devastated the country. Factional strife and isolation as the 'Hermit Kingdom' followed. Japan forced open its ports (1876), made Korea a protectorate in 1905 and annexed it in 1910.

name: Khmer Empire (Angkor)
rise: Jayavarman II declared independence from Java and himself universal monarch in 802 at Phnom Kulen.
fall: Overstretched water infrastructure, alternating mega-droughts and floods in the 14th–15th centuries, a shift to Theravada Buddhism and maritime trade, and attacks by Ayutthaya (1431) led the capital to move south.

name: Srivijaya
rise: Srivijaya emerged around 650 CE in Sumatra. The Chinese monk Yijing (671) found over a thousand monks studying there.
fall: The Chola king Rajendra I raided its ports in 1025. Later, Javanese Singhasari and Majapahit took over its role.

name: Pagan Kingdom
rise: Anawrahta united the Irrawaddy valley in 1044 and adopted Theravada Buddhism; over 10,000 temples, stupas and monasteries were built at Bagan.
fall: Overspending on temples, tax-exempt land and Mongol invasions in 1287 broke the kingdom.

name: Ayutthaya Kingdom
rise: U Thong (Ramathibodi I) founded Ayutthaya in 1351 on an island where three rivers meet, ideally placed for rice farming and for ships coming up the Chao Phraya. It absorbed Sukhothai, conquered Angkor in 1431, and developed the sakdina system that ranked every person by notional land rights. By the 17th century it was one of Asia's great ports, trading with China, Japan, Persia, the Dutch, French and English; the Greek adventurer Constantine Phaulkon became a royal minister under King Narai.
fall: Ayutthaya fought Burma for two centuries; it fell once in 1569 and was restored by King Naresuan, who won a famous elephant duel in 1593. In 1767 a Burmese army of the Konbaung dynasty besieged and burned the city after a 14-month siege, destroying temples, archives and the royal family. General Taksin rallied resistance from Thonburi within months, and in 1782 Rama I founded the Chakri dynasty at Bangkok, which still reigns.

name: Đại Việt (Lý and Trần)
rise: Lý Thái Tổ moved the capital to Thăng Long (Hanoi) in 1010 and founded the Temple of Literature (1070). The Trần (1225–1400), with General Trần Hưng Đạo, defeated three Mongol invasions, including at Bạch Đằng (1288).
fall: Hồ Quý Ly usurped the throne in 1400; Ming China invaded in 1407.

name: Majapahit
rise: Raden Wijaya used a Mongol invasion force to defeat his rival in 1293, then drove the Mongols out.
fall: Succession wars, the rise of Muslim port states such as Demak and Malacca, and Demak's conquest around 1527.

name: Malacca Sultanate
rise: Parameswara, a prince from Palembang, founded Malacca around 1400 and gained Ming Chinese protection; Zheng He's fleets visited. Conversion to Islam drew Muslim merchants, and Malacca controlled the strait trade in spices and textiles.
fall: Afonso de Albuquerque captured Malacca for Portugal in 1511; the sultan's heirs founded Johor and Perak.

name: Julio-Claudian dynasty
rise: Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium (31 BCE) and in 27 BCE took the title Augustus. He kept the forms of the Republic while controlling the army and provinces, ushering in the Pax Romana. His successors Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius (who invaded Britain in 43 CE) and Nero came from his family by adoption and marriage.
fall: Nero's extravagance, the Great Fire of Rome (64), the persecution of Christians and revolts in Judaea and Gaul led the Senate to declare him a public enemy; he took his own life in 68. The 'Year of the Four Emperors' (69) ended with Vespasian founding the Flavian dynasty.

name: Constantinian dynasty
rise: Constantine won at the Milvian Bridge (312), credited a Christian vision, issued the Edict of Milan (313), called the Council of Nicaea (325) and founded Constantinople (330).
fall: His sons fought each other; Julian 'the Apostate' tried to revive paganism and died campaigning in Persia in 363.

name: Carolingian dynasty
rise: Pepin the Short deposed the last Merovingian with papal approval (751). His son Charlemagne conquered Lombards and Saxons and was crowned emperor in Rome (800), fostering the Carolingian Renaissance of learning.
fall: Charlemagne's grandsons split the empire (Verdun, 843); Viking raids weakened them; Hugh Capet became king of France in 987.

name: House of Wessex and Anglo-Saxon England
rise: Alfred the Great (r. 871–899) of Wessex defeated the Danish Great Heathen Army at Edington (878) and built fortified towns (burhs) and a navy. His son Edward and daughter Æthelflæd, 'Lady of the Mercians', reconquered the Danelaw, and grandson Æthelstan became the first king of all England (927).
fall: Renewed Viking attacks under Æthelred the Unready led to Danish rule under Cnut (1016–35). Edward the Confessor died childless in January 1066; Harold Godwinson defeated a Norwegian invasion at Stamford Bridge but died at Hastings against William of Normandy.

name: Normans and Plantagenets
rise: William of Normandy won at Hastings in 1066, compiled the Domesday Book and built castles. Henry II founded the Plantagenet line (1154), ruling an 'Angevin empire' from Scotland to the Pyrenees. King John signed Magna Carta (1215).
fall: After the Hundred Years' War, the Wars of the Roses (1455–85) between Lancaster and York ended with Richard III's death at Bosworth.

name: Tudor dynasty
rise: Henry VII won at Bosworth (1485) and married Elizabeth of York to unite the rival houses. Henry VIII broke with Rome to annul his marriage (1534), dissolving monasteries; Elizabeth I's reign saw the defeat of the Spanish Armada (1588) and Shakespeare.
fall: Elizabeth I died unmarried in 1603, and the crown passed to James VI of Scotland, beginning the Stuart line.

name: Habsburg dynasty
rise: Rudolf I was elected King of the Romans in 1273; marriage alliances brought Burgundy, Spain, Bohemia and Hungary. Charles V (r. 1519–56) ruled an empire 'on which the sun never set'.
fall: Austria lost to Prussia (1866) and became Austria-Hungary (1867); the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand (1914) triggered World War I, and defeat dissolved the empire in 1918.

name: Bourbon dynasty (France)
rise: Henry IV, a Protestant who converted ('Paris is worth a mass'), became king in 1589 and ended the Wars of Religion with the Edict of Nantes (1598). Louis XIII and Cardinal Richelieu centralised power; Louis XIV (r. 1643–1715) built Versailles and made France Europe's dominant power.
fall: Costly wars, including support for the American Revolution, bankrupted the state. Louis XVI called the Estates-General in 1789; the Revolution abolished the monarchy in 1792 and executed him in 1793. Bourbons briefly returned (1814–30).

name: Romanov dynasty
notable: Peter the Great, Catherine the Great
rise: After the 'Time of Troubles', a Zemsky Sobor elected 16-year-old Michael Romanov tsar in 1613. Peter the Great (r. 1682–1725) modernised Russia, and Catherine the Great expanded to the Black Sea.
fall: Defeat in the Russo-Japanese War, the 1905 revolution, World War I disasters and food shortages led to the February Revolution of 1917; Nicholas II abdicated, and the Bolsheviks shot the family at Yekaterinburg in July 1918.

name: Hohenzollern (Prussia and Germany)
rise: The Hohenzollerns, electors of Brandenburg, became kings in Prussia in 1701. Frederick William I built a disciplined army, and Frederick the Great (r. 1740–86) seized Silesia and survived the Seven Years' War, making Prussia a great power. After defeat by Napoleon, reforms rebuilt it; Bismarck's wars with Denmark, Austria and France united Germany, and William I became German Emperor at Versailles in 1871.
fall: Kaiser William II dismissed Bismarck, pursued a naval race with Britain and backed Austria in July 1914. Germany's defeat in World War I and the November Revolution of 1918 forced William to abdicate and flee to the Netherlands; the Weimar Republic replaced the monarchy.

name: Macedonian dynasty (Byzantine)
rise: Basil I, a peasant-born groom who rose as a favourite of Michael III, had his patron murdered and took the throne in 867. His dynasty presided over the 'Macedonian Renaissance' in learning and art, the conversion of the Rus (988) and the reconquest of Crete, Cyprus and Antioch. Basil II 'the Bulgar-Slayer' (r. 976–1025) annexed Bulgaria.
fall: After Basil II's death the throne passed through the daughters Zoe and Theodora and their husbands; aristocratic factions and court intrigue weakened the army. When Theodora died in 1056 the dynasty ended, and within 15 years Byzantium lost Anatolia at Manzikert and southern Italy to the Normans.

name: Palaiologos dynasty
rise: Michael VIII Palaiologos, regent for a boy emperor of the Nicaean exile state, recaptured Constantinople from the Latin crusaders in 1261 and blinded the rightful heir to take sole power. He outmanoeuvred Charles of Anjou partly by financing the Sicilian Vespers revolt (1282). The dynasty ruled for nearly two centuries, presiding over a cultural 'Palaiologan Renaissance' of scholarship and mosaics such as those of the Chora church.
fall: The restored empire was poor and small; civil wars in the 14th century invited Ottoman mercenaries into Europe, and the Black Death struck in 1347. By 1400 Byzantium was little more than Constantinople. Constantine XI died defending the walls when Mehmed II's cannons breached them on 29 May 1453; the last Palaiologan outposts in the Morea fell by 1460.

name: Rurikid dynasty
rise: Rurik, a Varangian, reportedly came to rule Novgorod in 862; his successors ruled Kiev. After the Mongol conquest, the Muscovite branch rose; Ivan III ended Mongol tribute (1480) and Ivan IV crowned himself tsar (1547).
fall: Ivan IV killed his heir in a rage (1581); his son Fyodor I died in 1598 without children, beginning the Time of Troubles.

name: Piast and Jagiellonian Poland
notable: Casimir the Great, Władysław II Jagiełło
rise: Mieszko I accepted Christianity in 966, founding the Polish state; Bolesław I was crowned king in 1025. Casimir III the Great (r. 1333–70) codified laws and founded Kraków University. Queen Jadwiga married Lithuania's Grand Duke Jogaila (Władysław II Jagiełło) in 1386, creating a union that defeated the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald (1410).
fall: Sigismund II Augustus, last of the Jagiellonians, created the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth (Union of Lublin, 1569) but died childless in 1572, after which kings were elected by the nobility.

name: Old Kingdom of Egypt
rise: Building on the unification of Egypt around 3100 BCE, the Third Dynasty king Djoser and his architect Imhotep raised the Step Pyramid at Saqqara (c. 2670 BCE), the first monumental stone building. The Fourth Dynasty (Sneferu, Khufu, Khafre, Menkaure) built the Bent, Red and Giza pyramids, organising tens of thousands of paid labourers fed by state granaries. A powerful king ruled as a living god, supported by a vizier, scribes and provincial nomarchs.
fall: From the Fifth and Sixth Dynasties, royal power waned as nomarchs became hereditary and wealthy, and temples won tax exemptions. Pepi II's reign of perhaps 90 years ended in succession problems. Around 2200 BCE the '4.2-kiloyear event', a global drought, brought low Nile floods and famine; Egypt split into rival centres in the First Intermediate Period (c. 2181–2055 BCE).

name: New Kingdom of Egypt
rise: Ahmose I expelled the Hyksos around 1550 BCE. Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten (who tried to impose worship of the Aten) and Ramesses II built an empire into Syria and Nubia, with temples at Karnak, Luxor and Abu Simbel.
fall: After Ramesses III fought the Sea Peoples (~1175 BCE), the Bronze Age collapse, tomb robbing, and the rise of Amun priests at Thebes split Egypt by 1070 BCE.

name: Ptolemaic dynasty
rise: Ptolemy I, Alexander's general, took Egypt in 305 BCE; Alexandria's Library and Lighthouse were built.
fall: Cleopatra VII allied with Caesar and Antony, but defeat at Actium (31 BCE) and her suicide made Egypt a Roman province in 30 BCE.

name: Keita dynasty (Mali)
rise: Sundiata Keita defeated the Sosso at Kirina (1235). Mansa Musa (r. 1312–1337) made his famous hajj in 1324, so lavish with gold that he depressed its price in Cairo, and built mosques in Timbuktu.
fall: Succession disputes, Mossi and Tuareg raids and the rise of Songhai shrank Mali by the 1400s; the Keita lingered as local rulers until about 1670.

name: Solomonic dynasty (Ethiopia)
rise: In 1270 Yekuno Amlak overthrew the Zagwe dynasty, claiming descent from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba as recorded in the Kebra Nagast. Emperors such as Zara Yaqob reformed the church; in the 16th century Portuguese help saved Ethiopia from Ahmad Gragn's invasion. Menelik II defeated Italy at Adwa (1896), keeping Ethiopia independent.
fall: Haile Selassie modernised the state but faced famine, inequality and protests; the Marxist Derg military junta deposed him in 1974 and abolished the monarchy in 1975.

name: Zulu Kingdom
rise: Shaka (r. 1816–1828), a son of a minor chief, reorganised Zulu warriors into regiments (amabutho) armed with the short stabbing spear (iklwa) and large shields, using the 'bull's horns' encircling formation. In the turmoil of the mfecane he forged a kingdom of perhaps 250,000 people in what is now KwaZulu-Natal.
fall: Shaka was assassinated by his half-brothers in 1828. Under Cetshwayo, the Zulu defeated a British army at Isandlwana (January 1879) but lost at Ulundi in July. Britain split the kingdom into 13 chiefdoms, civil war followed, and Zululand was annexed in 1887 and joined to Natal in 1897.

name: Ashanti Empire
rise: Around 1701 Osei Tutu, with the priest Okomfo Anokye, united Akan states; tradition says the Golden Stool descended from the sky, embodying the soul of the nation. Kumasi controlled the gold and kola nut trade and the Atlantic slave trade.
fall: Seven Anglo-Ashanti wars (1823–1900) followed; Yaa Asantewaa led the 1900 War of the Golden Stool. Britain annexed Ashanti in 1901; the Asantehene remains a traditional ruler in Ghana.

name: Maya dynasties of Tikal
rise: Villages from about 2000 BCE became cities such as El Mirador in the Preclassic period.
fall: Classic southern cities were abandoned around 800–950 CE after droughts, warfare and overpopulation. Northern cities and highland kingdoms lasted until Spanish conquest (the last, Nojpetén, fell in 1697).

name: Aztec rulers (Tlatoani)
rise: The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan in 1325 and the Triple Alliance formed in 1428.
fall: Hernán Cortés, with tens of thousands of indigenous allies and a smallpox epidemic, besieged Tenochtitlan until it fell in 1521.

name: Inca Sapa Inca line
rise: Pachacuti (r. 1438–1471) turned the Cusco kingdom into an empire.
fall: Smallpox, a civil war between Huáscar and Atahualpa, and Pizarro's capture of Atahualpa at Cajamarca (1532).
